en: The Essential Heart-Mantra of the Thirty-Seven Honored Ones, Briefly Expounded for Vajraśekhara Yoga,
was taught by the Tripiṭaka Master Mahāprajña at the Daochang in the Chengming Hall of the Hanhuiyuan.

At that time, Vairocana Tathāgata, having arrived at the Peak Pavilion of the Sumeru Vajra Maṇi Jewel, was established by Vajradhātu Tathāgata—through the empowerment of all Tathāgatas—upon the lion thrones of all Tathāgatas, facing in every direction.

At that time, the Tathāgata Immovable of Great Bodhicitta, the Tathāgata Ratnasambhava of the Great Accumulation of Merit, the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvararāja of the Samādhi Treasury of Sublime Dharma, and the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi who Accomplishes All Activities—all these Tathāgatas empowered the Bhagavān Śākyamuni Tathāgata with their own bodies. Because he had thoroughly and equally realized all things, he sat facing the four directions, observing all quarters with impartiality.

Now, when a practitioner first gives rise to the mind of faith to manifest the *bodhicitta*, this is the *heruka* mind of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). It is the inner mind of sentient beings; one places the syllable *HŪṂ* as the seed-syllable. The transformation of this seed-syllable becomes a lunar disc (*candramaṇḍala*), within the radiance of which one visualizes a five-pronged vajra whose light shines through with clarity. This vajra is then transformed into Vajrasattva, who is another name for Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. This represents the Vajra Family of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya in the east, which is precisely the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.

Next, one should pay homage to the Tathāgata Ratnasambhava, the Accumulation of Merit in the South. Visualize him holding a *maṇi* jewel flask and conferring empowerment upon all Tathāgatas; he is the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, who holds a *maṇi* jewel and fulfills all the aspirations of sentient beings. Through this merit of the Accumulation of Virtue, with its immeasurable, boundless, and radiant majesty, all that is sought is swiftly fulfilled. This belongs to the Jewel Family (*ratnakula*) of the Tathāgata Ratnasambhava, which is the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*).

Next, one pays homage to the Tathāgata Amitābha of the western direction, who represents the *samādhi*-wisdom of all Tathāgatas. From the very first arousal of the bodhicitta, he is able to turn the wheel of Dharma; his eloquence is beyond verbal expression and his principle is boundless. He is included within the Speech Family (*vāk-kula*) and is able to cause sentient beings to attain clarity and sharp intelligence; this is that which is subsumed under the Western Dharma Family, namely the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*).

Next, one pays homage to the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi of the north. Through the skillful means of great compassion, he is able to accomplish all the activities of the Tathāgatas as well as the activities for sentient beings.
By means of the skillful wisdom and expedients of the Bodhisattva Viśvakarman, he is able to bring to ultimate fulfillment the bodhicitta of all sentient beings.
Without falling back, he sits at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and subdues all Māras; through many skillful means, he ensures that nothing can cause him to be discouraged or destroyed.

He is also able to transform empty space into a treasury, filling the entirety of space with precious jewels to make offerings to all Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of the ten directions. This Bodhisattva is the "Treasury of Empty Space" (Gaganagañja).
This is an alternative name for the Bodhisattva Viśvakarman; it is the seal (*mudrā*) accomplished through his vows and practices, which transmits the gateway to firm liberation.
It is the skillful means of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) that is well-able to protect and maintain the gateway of the three mysteries (*triguhyamukha*).
This is subsumed under the Karma Family (*karmakula*), namely the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*).
The ritual procedures for worshipping the Buddhas of the four directions, as well as the mantras, are fully explained in detail within the sutra.
It should be understood that among them, the Buddha Vairocana of the center is the Tathāgata Family.

The reward body (saṃbhogakāya) is perfected and adorned with myriad virtues; atop the summit of Mount Sumeru, within the precious peak pavilion and the great maṇi-jewel palace, he sits upon a vajra throne, attains equal and perfect enlightenment, and subdues all māras.
From every pore, he emits great radiance, and the Tathāgatas of the ten directions along with all the assemblies of sages come forth.
Those who have attained equal realization— the Bodhisattvas who have fulfilled the ten stages— all returned to this assembly and each took their seat in their respective original directions.
Abiding with minds in *samādhi*, from within the wisdom of the heart of Vairocana Tathāgata,
they brought forth immeasurable and boundless secret Dharma-gates, which are the samādhis corresponding to the Bodhisattva practice.
The mind of the yoga of perfected wisdom fills the dharma-realm;
this great bodhi is the perfection of the five wisdoms, namely the Tathatā-dharmadhātu-jñāna of Vairocana Tathāgata, which occupies the central position.
Next, one enters the stage of the samādhis of the sixteen great bodhisattvas.

Now, a practitioner of mantra must know that the sequences of the samādhis of the sixteen great bodhisattvas each differ, and that there are distinctions within the various aspects of the samaya-mind.

Furthermore, as for Vajrasattva, with the eastern direction as his head, he possesses the Great Bodhicitta; from the very first moment of generating the resolve, he is firm and courageous, abiding in the wisdom of samādhi. His self-enjoyment body is brilliantly radiant, shining extensively throughout the boundless [realms]. Grasping the five-wisdom vajra scepter, he occupies his seat with majestic pride and sovereignty—this is the nature of Vajrasattva.
The verse of the sutra says:
"How wondrous is the Great Samantabhadra!
The natural *sattva* of *sāra*, From the firm and bodiless, He has attained the body of *sattva*."
"Although he has realized the correct station of a *sattva*, his afflictions of view have not yet been eliminated; how then shall all sentient beings be guided and transformed?
He must practice the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to deliver them."
What are the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*)?
They are giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation, by which one gathers and attracts others.
Thus, the Bodhisattva Vajrarāja holds a pair of vajra-hooks to summon and attract them; this is the sublime function of the Bodhisattva Amogharāja.
The verse of the sutra says:
"How marvelous is the King of Non-Emptiness!
The hook born of the vajra, by pervading all Buddhas, is the most supreme means of summoning."
"Although there is summoning, it does not yet possess the mind of great compassion; one must instead give rise to affection for all sentient beings and exert oneself in their rescue and protection.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Vajraprema grasps the arrow of great compassion, which is capable of piercing the minds of the two vehicles that cling to conceptual attachments. If one cannot forget the 'if' and the 'not-yet,' how can one truly provide salvation and deliverance?"
Holding this bow and arrow of great compassion, one is also able to slay all afflictions and directly attain bodhi; this is the practice and stage of the Bodhisattva Vajrarāga.
The verse of the sutra says:
"How marvelous! The self-nature is pure, Yet it naturally follows along with defiled desire;
Because it is purified by being free from desire, It is tamed through defilement."

Through these supreme practices, he was exceedingly joyful and exclaimed, "Excellent! He immediately attained the three kinds of secret minds of all wholesome dharmas—excellent speech, excellent intention, and excellent body—and the three gates of wholesome dharma through which the three karmas were purified. He praised these excellent merits as immeasurable and boundless; this is the original account of the Bodhisattva "Excellent" (Sujāta).
The verse of the sutra says:
"How marvelous! How excellent am I, That I have been able to give rise to ultimate joy— A state free from all conceptualization, Attained through the supreme wisdom of all."
The above are the four bodhisattvas of the Vajra Family.

Because the fruits and vows resulting from these wholesome dharmas were not yet perfected, in an instant they were consecrated, their bodies adorned and embellished. They then became Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva, who holds a *maṇi* jewel flask. One should further visualize all Tathāgatas as the Great Bodhisattvas Who Bestow the Great *Maṇi* Jewel Consecration; they receive the position, and even when abiding in the station of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), they perform this for them all. Bringing benefit to beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, possessing a mass of boundless merit and sovereign majestic power—this is the merit and wisdom of Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva.
The verse of the sutra says:
"How wondrous is this sublime empowerment, The unsurpassed vajra jewel!
Because the Buddha is free from all attachment, He is named the Sovereign of the Three Realms."

"Although he has received the empowerment, he has not yet attained majestic radiance; he must obtain the full orb of the sun to illuminate the thousand worlds. Therefore, he holds the sun of adamantine light, which is blazing and brilliant, pure and penetrating without limit. Even if there were as many suns as atoms of dust, none could outshine or eclipse it; this is the pervasive illumination of the Bodhisattva Vajratejas."
The verse of the sutra says:
“How marvelous is this peerless light, Which illuminates the realm of sentient beings!
It is able to pacify and purify; To all these Buddhas, the saviors of the world.”
Since his radiance was vast and his meritorious achievements were most exalted, there must be gifts and offerings to reward and honor him.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja erected a great *maṇi* banner upon which he placed a wish-fulfilling jewel that emitted brilliant light. From it rained down hundreds of precious *maṇi* banners, canopies, silk streamers, and exquisite incense and flowers. He bestowed these as the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), fulfilling the needs of all sentient beings according to their wishes. Possessing a heart of great compassion, he gave away immeasurable treasures while remaining free from the notion of "giving," and attained a state of mind where nothing is gained; this is the power of the great compassionate vow of the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja.
The verse says:
"How marvelous is the peerless banner! It accomplishes all benefit for all;
it fulfills every intention and causes all vows to be fulfilled."

Having received this gift and benefit, his heart was filled with joy; he immediately attained a most extraordinary resolve. Speaking with delight and smiling with pleasure, his mind was set upon the joyful relinquishment that universally delivers sentient beings. His task being thus complete, this is the wondrous wisdom of joy of the Bodhisattva Vajrahasita.
The verse says:
"How marvelous! I laugh greatly; these Victors are most extraordinary.
They establish the benefit of the Buddhas while abiding eternally in sublime meditative equipoise."
The above are the four bodhisattvas of the Jewel Family (*ratnakula*). Although they are able to fulfill all wishes, they fear mental distraction (*vikṣepa*). This distraction consists of six types:

distraction of mental engagement (*manasikāra-vikṣepa*), distraction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikṣepa*), external distraction (*bahirdhā-vikṣepa*), internal distraction (*adhyātma-vikṣepa*), distraction of signs (*nimitta-vikṣepa*), and distraction of the seat (*āśraya-vikṣepa*). These are called the six types of distraction that cannot be restrained by the sovereign mind (*cittarāja*). One must therefore cultivate the methods of *samādhi* to stabilize the mind. Through the subtle principles of the sublime gateways of practice and the skillful means (*upāya*) of great compassion, which are likened to a raft, one suddenly realizes the causal practices and vows of ultimate enlightenment (*paramārtha-bodhicaryā-praṇidhāna*). This is precisely the compassionate wisdom of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
The verse says:
"How marvelous! My ultimate reality is primordially pure by nature;
all phenomena are like the parable of the raft, and thus purity can be attained."

Although he had realized the perfection of the Dharma, his fetters and afflictions (*kleśa*) had not yet been dispelled. Thereupon, the Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, whose *prajñāpāramitā* was perfected and whose wisdom was boundless, took up the sword of wisdom to sever the silken net. He eliminated the four Māras and the stubborn attachments of the two vehicles, abiding nowhere and dwelling neither in emptiness nor existence. Forever cutting off the two extremes, he was able to sever the minds of all sentient beings bound by their fetters. Constantly abiding in unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) wisdom that is perfectly luminous—this is precisely the wisdom of Mañjuśrī’s *prajñā*.
The verse says:
"How marvelous are all Buddhas! Having heard their subtle and wondrous voice, I realize that because wisdom is formless, it is through sound that it can be apprehended."

Through this, delusions are severed; thus, the sublime Dharma must be transmitted. This is the turning of the wheel of Dharma immediately upon the initial arousal of the bodhicitta. The Bodhisattva, abiding in the state of samādhi, gives rise to the vows and practices of great compassion and turns the true wheel of Dharma. The radiance of its spokes shakes the great trichiliocosm; the three spheres are purified, and he acts as the sovereign over all maṇḍalas. He issues commands to all māras and, through the samādhi of right reception, subdues sentient beings—this is the function of the wisdom-wheel of the Bodhisattva Vajramaṇḍa.
The verse says:
"How marvelous is the vajra-wheel! My supreme vajra-practice, by the mere arousal of the thought of enlightenment, is able to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma."
Once the Sublime Dharma has been turned, one must immediately enter the realm beyond words.

Since letters are fundamentally empty, the *sūtra* treasury of the True Suchness Dharma-realm is impartial; the *dharmaparyāya* of the *tathāgata* is perfected. Awakening to the Mahāyāna, there is nothing that is not expounded; through this supreme Dharma, one engages in discourse with all Buddhas. This is the Vinaya of recitation; truly, the entirety of the Mantras is contained herein.
This is the wisdom of the samādhi of the bodhisattva of non-speech, the wisdom of gnosis.
The verse says:
"How marvelous! My secret; I am named Secret Speech."
"The subtle and wondrous Dharma that has been taught is far removed from all conceptual proliferation. The above constitutes the section on the four Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Although they are common to the wisdom of speech, their buddha-activities and the activities for sentient beings have not yet been fully accomplished; thus, they enter the gateway of skillful means in all karmic functions to bring about realization. They extensively perform offerings and bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings, taking empty space as a treasury. Within it, precious jewels fill the entirety of space, providing relief to the masses and ensuring that the five kinds of giving never fail. They universally offer their hearts in worship to all the Tathāgatas and Buddhas throughout the ocean of lands as numerous as atoms in the ten directions; this is the skillful wisdom of the Bodhisattva Viśvakarman.
The verse says:
"How marvelous! I am not empty; I possess manifold karmas.
Without effort, I perform the Buddha-work and am able to transform adamantine karma."

Having completed these tasks, one should apply them with firm and steadfast diligence; for if one does not cultivate them with such vigor, Māra will find an opportunity to cause one to falter or retreat.
Therefore, don the armor of diligence, maintain the mind through the ten thousand practices, and guard the Dharma-gate so as not to fall back.

This is a vast and compassionate protection that can eliminate indolence and protect with firm and fierce wisdom; it brings about the ultimate realization of Bodhi instantaneously, leaving nothing unencompassed.
This is the great compassionate protection of the Bodhisattva Invincible Diligence.
The verse says:
"How marvelous is this firm armor! I am the one who is firmly armored;
through this firm armor of bodilessness, I have attained a firm body."

Once diligence is perfected, one must subdue the celestial māra, the skandha-māra, and the kleśa-māra. Manifesting in the form of a Vajrayakṣa, appearing fearsome, with blazing and radiant flames, wrathful and majestic, he holds a vajra-fang in his mouth. This is able to devour the beginningless ignorance and all dogmatic views of all sentient beings and utterly destroy them. Employing the skillful means of great compassion, he is even able to terrify all Tathāgatas; this is the wisdom of the skillful means of the Bodhisattva Vajrayakṣa’s great compassion.
The verse says:
"How marvelous is this great skillful means, the compassion of all Buddhas!
Through the tranquility of form, they manifest in the form of the wrathful."

"By means of this majesty and valor, the principle of liberation is brought to fulfillment; through the Secret Vajra, sentient beings at the limit of suffering within the three spheres are able to be delivered. By the empowerment of the three secrets of great skillful means and the mind-transmission of secret mudrās, one abides in samādhi and is able to untie the bonds of all essential dharmas. Delivering others from suffering and establishing them in bliss while dwelling in the four immeasurable minds—this is the wisdom of the Secret Seal of the Bodhisattva Vajramuṣṭi."
The verse says:
"How marvelous! My firm fetters, My firm samaya, because they fulfill all aspirations, Those who are liberated are bound."

The above constitutes the section on the ritual procedures (*karmavastu*) of the four Bodhisattvas. The Tathāgata Akṣobhya realizes the Vajra-pāramitā within his own mind and enters the empowerment of the Vajra-samaya of all samādhi-wisdoms. Because he experiences it for his own enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga*), from within the samādhi-wisdom of the five-crested radiant Vajra-bodhicitta, he emits vajra-light that pervades the worlds of the ten directions. This purifies the Great Bodhicitta of all sentient beings. Returning and gathering back into a single mass, in order to seal all Bodhisattvas and because he experiences the wisdom of his own samaya, he takes the form of the Bodhisattva Vajra-pāramitā. Holding a vajra, he dwells before the moon-disc of the Tathāgata Vairocana.
The verse says:
"How marvelous, all Buddhas! My body is the firm vajra;
because it is firm and without body, I have attained the vajra-body."

The Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava realized within his own mind the samādhi-wisdom of the Great Jewel-Treasury of Space (*ākāśaratnamahāmaṇigarbha-guṇa-samādhi-jñāna*). For the sake of his own enjoyment, from this samādhi-wisdom of the Great Jewel-Treasury of Space, he emitted the radiance of the space-jewel, which illuminated the worlds of the ten directions, causing the merit of all sentient beings to become perfect. It then returned and gathered into a single mass; in order to seal all Bodhisattvas and cause them to enjoy the wisdom of the *samaya*, it took the form of the Bodhisattva Vajraratnapāramitā, holding a great maṇi-jewel, and dwelt upon the moon-disc to the right of the Tathāgata Vairocana.
The verse says:
"How marvelous are all Buddhas! My name is Ratnavajra;
regarding the assembly of all seals, I am the firm principle of empowerment."

The Tathāgata Avalokiteśvararāja realized within his own mind the wisdom of the Great Lotus Wisdom Samādhi. For the sake of his own enjoyment, from that wisdom of the Great Lotus Wisdom Samādhi, he emitted lotus light that illuminated the worlds of the ten directions, purifying the adventitious afflictions of all sentient beings. It returned and gathered into a single mass; in order to seal all Bodhisattvas and for the sake of their enjoyment of the samaya of self-enjoyment wisdom, it took the form of the Bodhisattva Dharmapāramitā, holding a great lotus, and dwelt upon the moon disc behind the Tathāgata Vairocana.
The verse says:
"How marvelous! All Buddhas, the Dharma-vajra, and I are pure;
because of this natural purity, desire and passion are rendered stainless."

The Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi realized within his own mind the samādhi-wisdom of the Great Vīrya of Karma-vajra; for his own enjoyment, he emitted from that samādhi-wisdom of Karma-vajra Great Vīrya rays of karma-light that illuminated the worlds of the ten directions, causing all sentient beings to eliminate all indolence and achieve great vīrya. These rays returned and gathered into one mass, and in order to seal all bodhisattvas with the samaya-wisdom for his own enjoyment, he manifested in the form of the Bodhisattva Karma-pāramitā, holding a karma-vajra, and dwelt upon the moon disc to the left of the Tathāgata Vairocana.
The verse says:
"How wondrous are all Buddhas! I am the Vajra of manifold karma;
From one, I become all, Performing virtuous deeds within the Buddha-realm."

The above four pāramitās constitute the firm essence of the great bodhisattvas, which is like space and cannot be obstructed or destroyed. Just as flames, dust, clouds, and mist can obscure the realm of space, and even the light of the sun and moon may be hindered, so too all sentient beings—whose fundamental nature is originally pure—have their minds entangled and defiled by the two aspects of subject and object through adventitious afflictions, thereby failing to attain mastery. Now, this delusive conceptualization is empty in its very essence; realizing that all phenomena are unarisen, there is no obstruction between emptiness and existence.

Thereupon, Vairocana Buddha dwelt in the contemplation of the bodhicitta; his vision was thoroughly penetrating and perfectly luminous, flowing forth with sublime joy and manifesting various adornments and offerings. This is the wondrous function of the Great Bodhicitta of the Bodhisattva Vajrarati, who abides upon the lunar disc to the left of the maṇḍala of Akṣobhya Tathāgata.
The verse says:
"How marvelous is this peerless existence! Among all Buddhas, it is through the offering of defiled desire that one is able to transform all offerings."

"Now, having performed the offering of joyful play, Vairocana Buddha emanates from his inner mind a vajra-jewel garland to adorn his body; he gathers all manner of jewels to serve as ornaments, and with the radiance of these jewel-accumulations and the perfection of his merit, he fulfills the five kinds of vows and aspirations. He then dwells upon the moon disc to the left of the maṇḍala of the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava in the southern direction."
The verse says:
"How marvelous! I am peerless, Renowned as the Jewel of Offerings;
Supreme King of the Three Realms, I receive offerings through my teaching."

Having made this offering with the Jewel Garland, Vairocana then emanated from within his own mind the skillful means of great compassion; abiding in the state of samādhi, he uttered songs of praise and melodic recitations.

Having offered such worship, one attains the sixty-four kinds of Brahma-voices with unimpeded eloquence in preaching the Dharma; this voice is refined and pure, causing the multitude to delight in the music of flutes, lutes, and harps as an act of offering—this is precisely using sound as a Buddha-work.

The verbal expression of the Dharma-benefit is inherently empty in its essential nature; suchness is immovable and the dharma-realm is pure. This is the Vajragīta Bodhisattva’s speech-wisdom of offering, who dwells upon the lunar disc to the left of the Maṇḍala of the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvararāja.
The verse says:
"How marvelous! This has become a song of praise; I make offerings to all who see.
By virtue of these offerings, all dharmas resonate like echoes."

Although he was fully endowed with song and chant, he had not yet attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). Thereupon, from within the heart of Vairocana Buddha, there issued forth the activities of the Tathāgatas and the activities for sentient beings; he manifested skillful wisdom (*kauśalyajñāna*) and self-enjoyment wisdom (*svasaṃbhogajñāna*), performing various offerings and forming the extensive ritual of the *vajranṛtyamudrā*. Displaying great supernatural powers and adorned with wondrous dance as his buddha-activity, he made offerings to as many Buddha-fields as atoms while making offerings to as many Buddhas as grains of sand in the Ganges. He entered and emerged from the gates of samādhi without obstruction; this is the sublime function of the Bodhisattva Vajranṛtya, who dwells upon the lunar disc to the left of the Maṇḍala of the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi.
The verse says:
"How marvelous is this vast offering! Because all offerings are performed through the ritual of the vajra dance, the offering to the Buddha is established."
The above constitutes the inner offerings of the four Bodhisattvas.

From within the heart-mind of Tathāgata Akṣobhya, the Incense-Burning Bodhisattva flows forth to make offerings to Tathāgata Vairocana. The ocean-like clouds of incense pervade the entire Dharma-realm; those who see, hear, perceive, or know them are able to give rise to satisfaction and joy. This fragrance universally enters the bodies of all Buddhas, bringing delight and rapture; this is the performance of great Buddha-activities by the Vajra Incense-Burning Bodhisattva as an offering.
The verse says:
"How marvelous is this great offering! Radiant, moist, and endowed with perfect majesty;
through the universal entry of the sattva, one swiftly realizes awakening."
Having thus made offerings with incense, Ratnasaṃbhava Tathāgata causes exquisite flowers of awakening to flow forth from within his heart and presents them to Vairocana Tathāgata.

From the vajra-jewel lotus, its flower blooms with radiant light; its color is fresh and beautiful, adorned with various accumulations of merit, and it is able to bestow upon sentient beings the vow for peace and happiness—this is the sublime function of the Bodhisattva Vajrapuṣpa.
The verse says:
“How marvelous are all Buddhas, who are able to create every adornment!
Through the precious nature of the Tathāgata, they swiftly obtain offerings.”

Having already made offerings with flowers but not yet having attained radiant light, the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvararāja then caused a vajra-wisdom lamp to flow forth from within his heart; he used it to serve and make offerings to the Tathāgata Vairocana. Its light shone through with penetrating clarity, whereby he obtained the five pure eyes of a Tathāgata and beheld all internal and external forms without exception.

Within the lamp of inner wisdom, all phenomena are illuminated; their intrinsic nature is pure like a mani jewel, such that no hundred lights or thousand radiances can obscure it—the sun of wisdom arises from this very lamp.
This is the wisdom-illumination of the Bodhisattva Vajradīpa.
The verse says:
"How marvelous! I am vast, Making offerings with lamps that are sublime."
"By swiftly possessing radiant light, one attains the eye of all Buddhas.

Having thus made the offering of lamps, yet not having attained coolness, the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi then flows forth from within the heart as the Vajragandhā Bodhisattva; holding the incense mudrā, he makes an offering to the Tathāgata Vairocana.

This sublime unguent can eliminate the maladies of oppressive heat for all sentient beings; it enables one to attain the Tathāgata’s fivefold Dharma-body—of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—to adorn its very being, and furthermore, it allows one to realize the vast and perfect, cool and clear mind of Bodhi.
This is the offering of the Bodhisattva Vajragandha.
The verse says:
"How marvelous is this offering of fragrance! It is subtle, exquisite, and pleasing to my mind."
"By means of the fragrance of the Tathāgata, it is bestowed upon all bodies.
The above constitutes the external offerings of the four bodhisattvas.

Having completed the eight offerings, as the matters of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) were not yet perfected, the Vajrāṅkuśa Bodhisattva flowed forth from within the heart of Vairocana to summon them.
Now, the hook has four qualities of attraction: kind speech, giving, beneficial conduct, and cooperation; by means of these, it is able to ferry across immeasurable sentient beings.

Furthermore, it is that which can subdue the unruly hosts of Māras and control wild elephants so that they all become compliant; this very Great Bodhicitta is vast and perfect, firm and sharp, and resolutely non-retrogressive. It can also summon all the worthy sages to descend upon the site of practice, enabling all practitioners of *mantra* to swiftly realize *siddhi*. This is the wisdom of the Bodhisattva Vajrāṅkuśa for summoning.
The verse says:
"How marvelous! All Buddhas, you bind me with a firm pledge;
through my universal summoning, assemble all the maṇḍalas."

Having thus fulfilled the significance of the hook (*āṅkuśa*), yet not having completed the task of drawing forth and gathering [beings], the Vajrapāśa Bodhisattva flows forth from within the heart-mind of Vairocana Buddha. He is able to restrain all afflictions (*kleśa*), ignorance (*avidyā*), forgetfulness, and the darkened mind; he is able to bind all wheels of suffering (*duḥkhacakra*) so that they may attain liberation; and he is further able to induce meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the great bodhicitta. All the assemblies of mudrās gather together, and as many buddha-fields as there are atoms all descend upon the maṇḍala site to perform the buddha-work together.
The verse says:
"How marvelous are all Buddhas! My firm vajra-noose, even if it enters into all subtle atoms, shall draw them back into this once more."

Once the meaning of "seeking" (so) has been clarified, yet the principle of "restraint" (zhi) has not yet been applied, Vairocana Buddha then causes the Bodhisattva Vajraśṛṅkhalā to flow forth from within his heart. This "chain" (śṛṅkhalā) signifies the meaning of restraint; it is able to close the gates of all evil destinies. Arising with great compassion, he brings about protection for all sentient beings. He is able to bind all mudrās as well as the messengers of the Tathāgatas, all of whom attain Great Nirvāṇa through liberation.

Furthermore, he caused the ocean-like assemblies of Tathāgatas as numerous as atoms to abide in the state of samādhi within this site of enlightenment, performing great Buddha-activities together with the assembly of the Śrī-māyā-saṃbhava Buddha.
A verse says:
"How marvelous are all Buddhas, The great, firm diamond chain!"
"To cause those bound by fetters to be liberated, one binds oneself for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
Although it possesses the meaning of shackles and the function of restraint, it has entered universal principle and wisdom but has not yet attained perfect penetration.

Then, from within the heart-mind of Vairocana Buddha, there flows forth the Bodhisattva Vajraghaṇṭā, who holds a luminous bell as an offering. It produces immeasurable, subtle, and wondrous sounds; among all the holy assemblies, there are none who hear them and do not rejoice. The seed-syllable *Aḥ* of the Buddhas can universally enter the bodies and minds of all Tathāgatas, as clear as a bright mirror. Within the field of the bodies of immeasurable sentient beings, it is the great seed of wisdom; it is able to cast away its own body before the Buddhas to serve as a servant, attending to and making offerings to them. Within samādhi, it experiences delight and joy—this is the sublime resonance of the Bodhisattva Vajraghaṇṭā.
The verse says:
"How marvelous! All Buddhas, I enter the firm vajra;
I am the sovereign of all, and yet I am also their servant."
"This is the samaya of all Tathāgatas: summoning, causing entry, binding, and subduing.
Having bound the samaya-mudrā, it enables practitioners to find delight and peace within the ocean of Buddhahood—the samādhis of devas and humans—and thereby performs this offering."

Next, enter the ritual for making offerings to the five Tathāgatas. This involves entering the visualization of Vairocana Buddha and forming the seal of the Honored One, the All-Illuminating Tathāgata. Through this gateway of visualization, one’s body and mind become pure; bodhi is perfected, pervading the entire dharma-realm.
Next, enter the Vajrasattva Samādhi Seal to solidify the bodhicitta.
Next, enter the Great Jewel Seal of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha to obtain the fulfillment of all sentient beings' aspirations, free from any lack.
Next, enter the Lotus Samaya Seal of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; because of this purity and freedom from attachment, one obtains all supreme and subtle dharmas.

Next, he entered the samādhi of the Great Bodhisattva Karma, which is able to accomplish all the activities of the Tathāgatas; there is no practice among the activities of sentient beings that it does not bring to fulfillment.
These are Vairocana and the four great bodhisattvas, who are identical to the five Tathāgatas.

Next, one should practice the offerings of the sixteen great bodhisattvas; for the sake of making offerings, these great bodhisattvas each hold the seals (*mudrā*) of ritual implements, which they deploy upon the various limbs and members of their bodies, thereby performing great Buddha-activities for the Tathāgata.
First, Vajrasattva holds the seal of the five-wisdom vajra scepter to symbolize the firm and courageous bodhicitta.

Next is Vajrarāja Bodhisattva, who holds the seal of the double vajra hooks; by practicing the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), he summons all Tathāgatas and all sentient beings so that none fail to assemble like clouds, placing them at his right side as his emblem.

Next, bind the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Vajrarāga’s bow and arrow. This enables one to inspire love and affection in all sentient beings, and furthermore, it can shoot down the minds of those of the two vehicles who cling to views. Placing [the arrow] at the left side of the ribs, one employs it to remain unstained by any sensory forms or appearances.

Next, bind the mudrā of the Great Bodhisattva Sādhu-pramuditā. All Tathāgatas and the assembly of noble ones will all express their approval by snapping their fingers and praising with "Excellent! (Sādhu); place it behind the waist to signify this "Excellent."
The above constitutes the four great offerings of the Vajra Family.

Next, one should form the Great Jewel Seal of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, which is capable of fulfilling all that sentient beings seek so that they obtain it; placing it upon the forehead, it rains down various jewels, and one also holds a maṇi-jewel vase to confer empowerment upon all Tathāgatas.

Next, one should form the seal of the Great Bodhisattva Vajratejas; its majestic radiance is so brilliant that it can eclipse a thousand suns. Holding the vajra-sun, rotate it before you like the turning of the solar disc.

Next, bind the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja. Because of the wish-fulfilling jewel banner, it can fulfill all the aspirations and prayers of sentient beings; place it directly upward, as if it were a precious banner.

Next, bind the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Vajra-hāsa; this causes all the oceans of assemblies of worthy sages and Buddhas, as well as celestial seers and others, to be without exception filled with joy. Placing it above the mouth signifies great joyful laughter.
The above are the four offering Bodhisattvas of the Ratna family.

Next, one should enter the samādhi of the Padma family; by abiding in this visualization of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one can cause sentient beings to be unimpeded regarding all phenomena and free from defilement. Thereupon, one forms the Lotus mudrā and places it at the mouth, which is the manifestation of the pure sound of the Dharma.

Next, one should enter the contemplation of the wisdom of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. One should cause sentient beings to clarify the True Dharma and wield the sword of wisdom, thereby able to shatter the mountains of heterodoxy and sever the mind that clings to the views of the two vehicles. Abiding in the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—one should place [the image] at the edge of the right ear-wheel to dwell there as a place of rest.

Next, one should enter the visualization of the purity of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), which is capable of turning the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma. Having turned the Wheel of Dharma three times, one extensively delivers sentient beings throughout the three great trichiliocosms. This is the Bodhisattva Vajrahetu, who holds a vajra-wheel staff and places it at his left ear as his insignia.

Next, one should enter the Samaya of the Wordless. All phenomena are entirely beyond speech; the nature of speech is empty and primordially quiescent, such that there is nothing to be said. This is the Bodhisattva Vajra Speech, who holds the vajra tongue. One places it at the back of the crown of the head to symbolize the wordless.
The above constitutes the four sections on the Dharma of Approaching Bodhisattvas.

Next is the section on Activity (*karma-kula*), consisting of seventeen offerings. This is the Bodhisattva Vajrarati, who is able to bring joy and delight to sentient beings. Holding a three-pronged vajra, he places it upon his crown; he accomplishes all the activities of the Tathāgatas, and all the activities of sentient beings are fully accomplished.
Next is the activity of the adornment by the Vajramālā mudrā; it is adorned with a precious garland of nooses formed from various jewels, and this mudrā is placed upon the forehead.

Next is the Bodhisattva Vajragīta, who is able to accomplish the sixty-four kinds of Brahma-sounds for the Tathāgata’s songs, praises, and chants, all of which become sublime. Holding the seal of the vīṇā upon his right shoulder, every sound he utters becomes the wondrous Dharma.

Next is the Bodhisattva Vajranṛtya, who possesses sovereign supernormal powers and manifests transformations throughout the ten directions; every movement and action is nothing other than a Buddha-activity.
These four bodhisattvas are the four Great Bodhisattvas of the Northern Quarter who attend [the Buddha], and they are governed by the Karma family.

Next, one binds the mudrās of the outer offering bodhisattvas: namely, the Vajra Incense, the Vajra Flower, the Vajra Lamp, and so forth, up to the Vajra Unguent Bodhisattvas, who constitute the seventeen miscellaneous offerings; the Vajra Jewel Seal offering can fulfill the aspirations of sentient beings. One should then offer with the subtle and wondrous sounds of the Dharma through vajra music, song, praise, recitation, flutes, lutes, and harps.

Next, one binds the Kalpavṛkṣa mudrā, which can cause all sentient beings to fulfill their most excellent aspirations. Whatever they require—hundreds of thousands of precious jewels, playthings, famous garments, or superior robes—all shall be fully satisfied within this tree, without any lack or deficiency.

Next, bind the Karma-Samaya mudrā and constantly maintain this contemplation: "In the expanse of space, I serve and make offerings to all the Tathāgatas; before each and every Buddha, I imagine this very body of mine prostrating and making offerings."

Next, one should enter the Dharma Samaya Mudrā and constantly reflect: "This body of mine is now equal to the bodies of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. One should contemplate the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), which is without distinction and possesses no further differing characteristics; it is identical to the bodies of all Tathāgatas.
The above constitutes the method for practicing *samādhi*.

Next, one practices the method of the six *pāramitās* to deliver sentient beings; by cultivating the four immeasurable minds and making great vows, one shall give rise to the bodhicitta and immediately attain realization.

Next, one enters the contemplative practice of the six pāramitās. As for the dāna-pāramitā, it belongs to the Jewel Family; thus, by means of non-abiding generosity, one fulfills the wishes of all sentient beings throughout the expanse of space according to their desires, bestowing everything they seek upon them.

Furthermore, within the midst of birth and death, out of compassion for sentient beings, they act to rescue and protect them, causing all to be fully satisfied; they are also able to guard the bodhicitta, delivering those not yet delivered and bringing peace to those not yet at peace. They can also rain down various kinds of precious jewels, bestowing them extensively upon sentient beings to make them complete in wealth, happiness, and abundance, thereby enabling them to attain liberation.

The perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) consists of the three clusters of pure precepts: first, the precept of restraining from misconduct; second, the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas; and third, the precept of benefiting sentient beings, also known as the precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*).

All practices of the precepts are encompassed within the governance of the *vinaya* (disciplinary code). By virtue of upholding the precepts, one obtains the retribution of purity in body, speech, and mind; this is identical to the Tathāgata Vairocana’s body that fills the dharma-realm, the essence of suchness (*tathatā*), and is also termed the "merit of cessation" (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).

Regarding the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharmasaṃgrāhaka-śīla*): all wholesome dharmas are subsumed within this precept, which is also called "Wisdom-Virtue" (*jñānaguṇa*). This is precisely the Perfect Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) of Vairocana Tathāgata, adorned with physical marks and radiant with brilliant light; seated upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, he expounds the Mahāyāna sūtras for the sake of all bodhisattvas.

That which benefits sentient beings is precisely the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni. Because the Tathāgata, out of compassion for sentient beings in this world, manifests various skillful means as an emanation body to rescue and deliver them so that they may reach the other shore, this is termed "beneficent virtue."
In summary, according to the meaning of these three virtues, they are all subsumed and transformed by the *śīla-pāramitā*.
As for the *kṣānti-pāramitā*, it has five meanings: first, the patience of subduing (*avaivartika-kṣānti*);

second, the patience of faith (*adhimukti-kṣānti*); third, the patience of conformity (*anuloma-kṣānti*); fourth, the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); and fifth, the patience of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa-kṣānti*).

The伏忍 (Furěn, Patience of Submission) corresponds to the East; the信忍 (Xìn'rn, Patience of Faith) corresponds to the South; the順忍 (Shùn'rn, Patience of Accordance) corresponds to the West; the無生忍 (Wúshēng'rn, Patience of Non-arising) belongs to the North; and the寂滅忍 (Jìmíè'rn, Patience of Quiescence) corresponds to the Center. Within these five directions, there are thus the Five Tathāgatas.

The three stages of worthiness prior to the grounds involve the patience of subduing (*kṣānti*); furthermore, the first, second, and third grounds are assigned to the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*), while the fourth, fifth, and sixth grounds are assigned to the patience of conformity (*anuloma-kṣānti*). The seventh, eighth, and ninth grounds are assigned to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and the tenth ground, being fully perfected, is likewise assigned there. The stages of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and Subtle Wondrous Enlightenment (*pratyeka-buddha*) are assigned to the patience of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa-kṣānti*).

By virtue of upholding the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), in whatever place one is born, one attains the karmic fruit of physical beauty and is surrounded by a retinue; one’s merit becomes vast, immeasurable, and boundless, inexhaustible; and all who see or hear of one rejoice, respectfully comply with them, and follow their will with delight—this is the characteristic mark of the practice of the perfection of patience.

Regarding the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*): if a person practices but is unable to apply themselves with diligent effort and ascetic practice to seek liberation, Māra will immediately find an opportunity; they will fall into the ocean of birth and death in the hells, circling through the six realms of existence with no means of escape.

Therefore, one must don the armor of diligence to crush the demon of indolence; through the refined cultivation of the myriad practices, all are fully accomplished. One’s majestic virtue becomes sovereign like the sun, for the three thousand dignified postures and eighty thousand subtle conducts all arise from upholding this precept—this is the characteristic of the practice of the Perfection of Diligence.

Regarding the *dhyānapāramitā*: when ordinary people practice, their minds are often distracted due to conceptualization, which prepares six kinds of mental agitation that entangle the body and mind. Because mindfulness is thus unsettled, they cannot attain liberation; therefore, one must cause the mind to dwell on a single object and no longer attend to other objects.

Among the four types of dhyāna, one abides in the Tathāgata’s pure dhyāna, forever eliminating delusive thoughts. One must abide in the "abiding of non-abiding," constantly relying on a mind free from conceptualization. The true mark (*dharmatā*) is perfectly luminous, pervading the entire Dharma-realm; the path to Great Bodhi is thereby attained—this is the perfection of dhyāna (*dhyānapāramitā*).

Regarding the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*): "wisdom" (*jñāna*) refers to the capacity for discernment, while "insight" (*prajñā*) arises from analytical clarity. Just as a bright mirror can reflect all forms without error, so too do the teachings of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna remain free from discrepancy. By eliminating the two marks of self-clinging and abiding in the mind of the Mahāyāna, one brings bodhi to fulfillment, realizes the limit of suchness (*tathatā*), and attains the Tathāgata’s equal dharmakāya.

When the practitioner binds the seals of the six pāramitās, recites the mantras of the six pāramitās, and dwells in the contemplative gateway of the six pāramitās, they are identical to the suchness-wisdom of liberation of all Tathāgatas.

The Dharmakāya, by means of these six kinds of skillful means, enters the three gates of liberation—namely, the gates of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). All phenomena (*dharmas*) are entirely empty in their very essence; there is not a single thing that is not true, nor a single object that is not real. This is the wondrous existence of true emptiness, the perfect clarity of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). To recite the *Om ye dharmā* mantra is precisely the perfectly integrated wisdom of the essential body of Vairocana Tathāgata.

By virtue of this supreme meaning, one should then form the Tathāgata’s mouth-seal (*mudrā*), abide in the contemplation of the three gates of secret activity, and recite the mantras of the three secrets; thus, all sentient beings will without exception attain liberation.

The essential Dharma teachings thus produced are dedicated to all sentient beings, so that through seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, they may all transcend the three realms. One should seal the four great seals, recite the four kinds of mantras, and chant the hundred-syllable vidyā. Abiding in the mind of samādhi, one holds the rosary and performs the recitation; when the recitation is complete, one chants various praises and offers various named flowers. Reciting the hundred-syllable mantra, one immediately enters the ocean of Buddhas within the dust-motes of all lands, expanding the movement of the mind to its vastest extent.

Once the ritual of offerings is completed, one should first perform the mudrās of the thirty-seven deities of the preceding *karman*; thereafter, one should form the *samaya* seals and the sixteen great offerings, up to the seventeen miscellaneous offerings. Following this, one presents the *argha* water, performs the dedication of merit and makes vows, and then enters the *samaya*. Abiding in the state of *samādhi* through the gate of visualization, one recites the mantra while walking in circumambulation (*caṅkrama*).
In moments of rest, I turned my reading to Mahāyāna sūtras such as the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Laṅkāvatāra*, contemplating the Buddha-way.

The National Preceptor, the Great Tripitaka Master, while at the Great Place of Practice (Mahāmaṇḍala) in the Chengming Hall of the Hanhui Court, took advantage of a brief interval from his duties to peruse Sanskrit scriptures. His face beamed with joy; he found sublime delight in the Dharma, opening the gate of great compassion to guide the ignorant. Having established this excellent condition for the future, he enabled me to perceive that my secret teaching is vast and boundless, and that the subtle essence of the Dharma-body is truly difficult to fathom. Now, following the traces of the Yoga teachings, I shall briefly provide a guide. Regarding the gateway of mantra practice, I shall here reveal its underlying principle: that which contemplates is the Reward Body (Sambhogakāya) of Vairocana Buddha, and that which is contemplated is the Tathāgatas of the Four Wisdoms.
That which is able to observe these Tathāgatas of the four directions is the observer, while that which is observed is the sixteen great Bodhisattvas.
That which is able to observe this mind is the observer, while that which is observed is the object.

Regarding the eight offering goddesses and the four great protective Bodhisattvas, each possesses both the subject and the object; yet, although they possess subject and object, the essence of subject and object is fundamentally empty. The principle of emptiness and existence is fundamentally non-existent, and thus the mind of the Middle Way is realized.

Now, this established Great Maṇḍala of the Thirty-seven Honored Ones of the Vajradhātu, along with the twenty and forty deities of the Outer Vajra Family of the Thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, constitutes the primary source from which infinite maṇḍalas are produced in successive succession.

Now, I shall further establish the ritual rules for subduing through the thirty-seven deities of the Trailokyavijaya Wrathful Maṇḍala Assembly. From Mañjuśrī up to the various celestial beings of the Vajra Division, this method differs slightly from other teachings; I shall briefly describe and point it out based on its cultivation and realization. Within the *samaya*-mind, one enters and exits without obstruction, refining the wisdom-mind (*prajñā*) and abiding in the bodhicitta. Expanding boundlessly, it pervades the entire dharma-realm. When gathered, one immediately enters within the peak of vajra-light; when emerging into space, one fills the ocean-like assemblies of Tathāgatas as numerous as atoms throughout the void, where they all come together to realize the truth and transmit the mind-seal (*cittamudrā*). They then indicate the subtle gate of contemplation, taking the Vajrayāna as the essential core.

Furthermore, it is said that the method of *homa* yields inexhaustible benefits; whatever rites one performs must be received from a master. The number of hearths and the nature of the altar vary according to their specific purposes. Ghee, honey, and firewood all serve sublime functions, while the offerings of incense, medicinal herbs, and food, as well as the rules for pacification (*śāntika*) and subjugation (*abhicāruka*), are likewise distinct. The addition of phrases to the mantras and the ritual procedures for entering the maṇḍala all follow their respective families (*kula*), and thus they do not share the same principle.
This present exposition is intended to sever all doubts; by practicing in accordance with it, one will certainly be free from error.

Although I wish to explain this extensively according to the sūtras, the meaning is so profound that it is difficult to fully express. While other ritual protocols are fully contained within the sūtras themselves, I shall here briefly set forth the essential gateways for the cultivation of the thirty-seven deities of the Vajradhātu, unfolding them in a continuous, interconnected sequence.

Having received this gift of the Dharma, we disciples are filled with profound joy and exultation; with single-minded devotion and reverence, we stand waiting to listen, transcribing word for word as it is spoken and recording it privately.

Next, regarding entry into the gates of liberation—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*): as for emptiness, all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty; the essence of emptiness is also empty, and even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended.

Regarding "signlessness": the signs of earth, water, fire, wind, male, female, and so forth, as well as blue, yellow, red, and white—within these ten signs, all phenomena (*dharmas*) are entirely empty in their very substance, because all signs are empty and unapprehendable.

Regarding wishlessness (*apraṇihita*): whatever path one cultivates, one must sever the mind that harbors hope for the three realms. Since all that is sought through wishing possesses marks (*nimitta*), one must forever sever deluded thoughts and cut off the mind of seeking and desiring. To be without wish and without seeking is true liberation.
Because these three characteristics are empty, one enters the gateway of liberation.

Upon awakening to this correct principle, the body immediately possesses a radiance that pervades the entire dharma-realm; this is identical to the Perfect Essential Wisdom (*samyak-svabhāva-jñāna*) of Vairocana. All of this arises from reciting the *Om va~* mantra and forming this secret mudrā, whereby one enters the gateway of liberation through the contemplation of the Three Mysteries. With a single object and a single mind, one shall realize and awaken.

Next are the three secret oral mudrās; through these three secrets, the three karmas are purified. One contemplates this body as filling the entire dharma-realm, wherein every atom is all the Buddhas. Before each and every Buddha, there is one's own self, prostrating, serving, making offerings, repenting, and making vows at the feet of all the Buddhas.

Regarding the four great seals: first, as for Vajrasattva, one visualizes the five-pronged vajra always resting upon the lunar disc of the bodhicitta; from that vajra, immeasurable light radiates, which is itself the wisdom-mind of enlightenment.

The second jewel-seal is the vajra-mass of merit of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha; its precious jewels are inexhaustible, and it can also confer empowerment upon all Tathāgatas and fulfill the vows of sentient beings.

Next, through this mudrā, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva is able to purify the *dharmadhātu* and enter the gate of wordless contemplation; observing the brilliant radiance of the five wisdom-vajras upon his tongue, he preaches the Dharma without obstruction, thereby entering the *paramārtha-bodhicitta-mudrā*.

Regarding the fourth, the Karma-mudrā: visualize the Karma-vajra-ghaṇṭā (vajra-bell) and form this bell-seal within the lunar disc. Rotate it upon the heart center so that its wheel fills the entire Dharmadhātu. All the vows of the Buddhas are thereby fulfilled; service and offerings are performed without deficiency. Furthermore, one becomes identical with all Buddhas, and all offerings bring their aspirations to full realization. This is the shared activity of the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja.
The above six sections were personally finalized and translated at the presence of the Acharya.
This "Brief Exposition of the Essential Points of the Thirty-Seven Deities of the Vajradhātu Yoga" was punctuated on the fifteenth day of the fifth month of the third year of the Jōkyō era.

The original woodblock edition contained many errors, rendering the meaning of the text difficult to discern; I have therefore applied punctuation and annotations to the extent of my humble understanding. I pray that future gentlemen will seek out superior editions to collate and correct this work.
Jingyan, a disciple of the Vajrayāna in Henan, [practiced] for forty-eight years.
